ATP synthase. A molecular turbine that harnesses proton gradients across membranes to drive ATP synthesis from ADP and inorganic phosphate. It couples chemiosmotic potential energy, created by electron transport chains, into high-energy phosphate bonds, powering nearly all cellular work. ATP synthase catalyzes the reaction where ADP and inorganic phosphate combine to form ATP, and under certain conditions this reaction reverses to regenerate ADP and phosphate. The mechanism is a proton-powered rotary system. Proton flow through the enzyme rotates a rotor subunit, driving conformational changes that close around ADP and phosphate, facilitating phosphorylation. The structure consists of an F-zero component spanning the membrane as a proton channel and an F-one catalytic head. It resembles a nano-scale electric motor with rotor and stator components. ATP synthase is located on the inner mitochondrial membrane in eukaryotes, the plasma membrane in prokaryotes, and the thylakoid membrane in chloroplasts. The proton gradient is driven by the electron transport chain in mitochondria and by light-driven water splitting in chloroplasts. The energy source is the electrochemical gradient, with approximately three protons per ATP in mammals and approximately four in plants and bacteria. The rotor spins between one hundred and three hundred times per second, making it among the fastest rotating nanomachines in nature. ATP synthase is arguably the most important enzyme in energy metabolism. It is responsible for producing the ATP that powers life's cellular processes. Evolution converged on a rotary mechanism because it elegantly couples a concentration gradient to chemical bond formation. The enzyme's discovery, particularly the rotary mechanism revealed by single-molecule experiments in the nineteen nineties, was revolutionary. Scientists could visualize the molecular machine spinning under a microscope.
